cards.title: Two locks on the door
cards.body:
Even a great password can be stolen, for example in a [[data breach]] or by a fake website.

So many accounts let you add a **second lock**. Then a stolen password on its own isn't enough to get in.

cards.title: What two-step sign-in is
cards.body:
**Two-step sign-in** means proving it's you in two different ways. You'll also see it called **two-factor** or **multi-factor authentication (MFA)**. The proofs come in three kinds:

- something you **know**: a password or PIN
- something you **have**: your phone, or a small security key
- something you **are**: your fingerprint or face

cards.prompt: Sort each proof: something you **know**, **have** or **are**.

items.label: Your phone with an authenticator app
A security key on your keyring

cards.explanation: Passwords and PINs are things you **know**. Your phone and a security key are things you **have**. Fingerprints and faces are part of who you **are**. Two-step sign-in uses two different kinds.
cards.hint: Ask of each one: is it in your head, in your pocket, or part of your body?
cards.nudge: For each one, ask where it lives: in your head, in your pocket or bag, or as part of you.

cards.title: Which second proof is strongest?
cards.body:
Strongest first:

1. A **[[passkey]]**: your device signs you in with your fingerprint, face or PIN, and it won't work on a fake website.
2. A code from an **[[authenticator app]]** on your phone.
3. A code sent by **text message** (SMS), which can be intercepted.

Old-style **security questions**, like "What was your first pet's name?", are weak: the answers can often be guessed or found online.

When you turn two-step sign-in on, save the **backup codes** it gives you somewhere safe, in case you lose your phone.

cards.title: Never share a sign-in code
cards.body:
A sign-in code is the second key to your account. **No real company, bank, game or friend will ever ask you to read it out or send it to them.**

If someone asks for a code, it's a scam. And if a code arrives that you didn't ask for, someone may already know your password: change it.

cards.prompt: You're watching a video when your phone buzzes.

steps.text: A text arrives: **"Your sign-in code is 481 902."** You weren't signing in to anything. What does it probably mean?

choices.text: Someone knows my password and is trying to sign in
choices.consequence: Right. The code stopped them, but they have your password.
Codes are sent when someone tries to sign in. Someone tried, and it wasn't you.

steps.text: A minute later, a message from a friend's account: **"Oops, I sent you my code by mistake! Can you send it back?"**

choices.text: Send the code, to be helpful
choices.consequence: That was the attacker. The code was for **your** account, and now they're in.

choices.text: Don't send it. Change your password, and warn your friend another way
choices.consequence: The attacker has no way in, and your friend learns their account was taken over.

cards.explanation: A code you didn't ask for means someone has your password: **change it**. Never send a sign-in code to anyone, even a friend. Their account may have been taken over.
cards.hint: Codes arrive when someone tries to sign in. And remember the rule: nobody real ever asks you to send them a code.

cards.prompt: Which second proof is the **hardest** for an attacker to steal?

options.text: A code sent by text message
options.nudge: Text codes are better than nothing, but they can be intercepted or talked out of you. Look for the one listed as strongest.

options.text: A security question like your first pet's name
options.nudge: Answers like your pet's name can often be found or guessed from what you post. Look for proof that uses your device.

cards.explanation: A **passkey** is the strongest: your device proves it's you, and it won't work on a fake website. A text code is weaker, and a security question is the weakest of these three, because the answer can be guessed or found.
cards.hint: Think back to the list: strongest first, and what it said about security questions.

cards.title: Password managers
cards.body:
A **password manager** is an app that creates a **long random password** for every account, remembers them all, and fills them in for you. Many phones and browsers have one built in.

You only remember **one main password**: make it a strong passphrase, and protect the manager with two-step sign-in.

Bonus: it fills in passwords only on the **real** website. If it doesn't offer your password, check the address carefully: you might be on a fake site.

cards.prompt: Match each one to what it does.

pairs.right: Remembers a different password for each account
A second proof as well as your password
Signs you in with your device and fingerprint, face or PIN

cards.explanation: A **passphrase** is long and memorable, a **password manager** keeps one password per account, **two-step sign-in** adds a second proof, a **passkey** signs in with your device, and a **sign-in code** is never shared.
cards.hint: Start with the ones you're surest of. Two of them are about remembering passwords, and three are about signing in.
cards.nudge: A passphrase is something you make up; a password manager is an app. A code is the one you must never share.

cards.prompt: Put these ways to sign in in order, from **strongest** to **weakest**.
cards.explanation: A **passkey** is strongest, then a password with an **authenticator app**, then a password with a **text code**. A password alone is the weakest: one leak and it's open.
cards.hint: The lesson listed the second proofs strongest first. And any second proof beats none.
cards.nudge: A password with any second proof beats a password on its own. Among the second proofs, remember the order from the lesson.

cards.prompt: Your phone, with your authenticator app on it, falls in a lake.

steps.text: You try to sign in on a laptop, and it asks for the code from the app. What can you use?

choices.text: One of the backup codes you saved when you set it up
choices.consequence: You're in. Now set two-step sign-in up again on your new phone.

choices.text: Ask the website to switch two-step sign-in off for good
choices.consequence: That leaves your account with one lock. Use the backup codes you saved.

choices.text: Ask someone online who says they can get you in
choices.consequence: Anyone offering to get into accounts for you is a scammer.

cards.explanation: That's why you save **backup codes** when you turn two-step sign-in on. Keep them somewhere safe, like in your password manager or printed at home.
cards.hint: When you turned two-step sign-in on, it gave you something to save for exactly this moment.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Two-step sign-in** adds a second proof: something you know, have or are.
- Strongest: a **passkey**, then an [[authenticator app]], then a text code. Save your **backup codes**.
- **Never share a sign-in code.** One you didn't ask for means: change your password.
- A **password manager** keeps a different strong password for every account.

That's your accounts locked. Next module: spotting scams.
